CVE-2026-114114.description: Vyper 0.1.0b1 before 0.1.0b12, 0.1.0b14, and 0.4.1 through 0.5.0b1 mix character-based line offsets with Python's UTF-8 byte col_offset values in vyper/ast/parse.py, so multi-byte characters shift the source slices used to reconstruct later numeric literals. An attacker contributing source with non-ASCII identifiers that NFKC-normalize to ASCII, or an invisible byte-order mark, can silently substitute addresses, integers or other constants in compiled code.

CVE-2026-114115.description: Vyper 0.3.8 through 0.5.0b1 contains a compiler miscompilation vulnerability in parse_IfExp that reads nested arrays with narrower inner bounds using the wider result type's memory layout. When a ternary selects the narrower array, inner arrays after the first are read at wrong offsets, causing contracts to silently store corrupted values or revert.

CVE-2026-114116.description: Vyper 0.1.0b1 before 0.1.0b17 and 0.4.1 through 0.5.0b1 builds its source-line table with str.splitlines(), which treats characters like form feed and U+2028 as line breaks the Python parser ignores, so numeric literals are classified and validated from shifted source text. An attacker contributing source code can hide these characters in comments, strings or indentation to silently change address, integer or decimal constants.

GHSA-2489-32vh-8rrc.title: Function variables can replace imported constant values and default arguments
GHSA-2489-32vh-8rrc.description: ## Summary Vyper can resolve names inside unfoldable constants and omitted default arguments against the function using them rather than their original declaration in an imported module. A same-named parameter, local, or loop variable can silently replace the intended value, including with values outside the declared type's range. ## Details These expressions are typechecked where declared but compiled at their use site. In `vyper/codegen/expr.py`, `parse_Name` checks `context.vars` before using the name's semantic binding. Consequently, a variable in the using function can override a reference that was validated as a module constant or immutable. Unfoldable constant values are expanded by `parse_Name` and `parse_Attribute`. Omitted internal defaults are compiled through `Expr(default, context)` in `self_call.py`; external defaults are similarly compiled in the function's context by `external_function.py`. The colliding declaration must live in an imported module: declaring the constant and same-named parameter in one module fails with `NamespaceCollision`. Expansion is recursive, so qualifying the outer constant as `lib.CS` does not protect bare names inside its value. Constant and internal-default expansion can capture in-scope parameters, locals, or loop variables; external defaults can capture parameters through expanded imported constants. The replacement can also bypass type constraints: primitive setters trust internally encoded values and do not necessarily clamp them to the destination type. The using function's `uint256` word can therefore enter a nominal `uint8` slot unchanged. Fully folded expressions avoid the name lookup and are unaffected by this trigger. ## Proof of concept ```vyper # lib.vy struct S: a: uint8 E: constant(uint8) = empty(uint8) CS: constant(S) = S(a=E) @internal @pure def f(x: uint8 = E) -> uint8: return x ``` ```vyper # main.vy import lib @external @pure def test(E: uint256) -> (uint256, uint256): return convert(lib.f(), uint256), convert(lib.CS.a, uint256) ``` Both results should be `0`. Instead, `test(300)` returns `(300, 300)`: the function parameter `E` replaces the library binding, and the value survives despite the nominal `uint8` type. ## Impact The using function's variables can replace module-defined defaults or constants used in validation, routing, flags, or accounting. An external user controls the replacement only when the captured variable depends on user input, as in the PoC. The name collision is part of the developer-written source. Values outside narrow integer ranges and noncanonical booleans can propagate internally or appear in ABI output. Exploitation requires a matching name and an expression that remains unfoldable; consequences depend on how the contract uses the captured value. ## Affected versions The issue affects versions from **0.4.0b1 through master (at `17e925db`) ## Remediation Preserve declaration bindings when compiling constant values and default arguments, rather than resolving their names through the using function's local scope. Also enforce primitive type compatibility and destination constraints during internal assignments. As a workaround, use literal or fully folded values, or avoid collisions with names throughout the expanded expressions. Explicitly passing a qualified immutable can avoid default capture; qualifying an unfoldable constant alone is insufficient. Deployed contracts may require recompilation and redeployment or an upgrade.

GHSA-6j9c-gvcw-74fj.title: Optimizer replaces `msg.value | K` and `len(msg.data) | K`with `1` in ternary branches
GHSA-6j9c-gvcw-74fj.description: ## Summary With optimization on (`-O gas`, the default, or `-O codesize`), `(msg.value | K)` used as a branch of a ternary expression compiles to the constant `1`, whatever amount was sent. `K` is any nonzero integer literal. `len(msg.data) | K` is affected the same way. There is no warning or revert. `-O none` produces the correct value. ## Details The optimizer rewrites `(or x K)` to `1` (`vyper/ir/optimizer.py:396-398`). This is only valid where the result is used for its truthiness, i.e. as a condition. Whether a node is in such a position is decided from its parent's opcode alone (`optimizer.py:242`). As a result, both value branches of an `if` are treated as if they were the condition. For most operands, `finalize` rolls the rewrite back. It does not for `callvalue` and `calldatasize`: both are in `do_not_cache` (`codegen/ir_node.py:392`), so `is_complex_ir` does not treat them as complex. ## PoC ```vyper @external @payable def f(c: bool) -> uint256: return (msg.value | 2) if c else 5 ``` `f(True)` with `msg.value = 5` returns `1` at the default level and `7` at `-O none`. The IR at the default level: ``` [if, [iszero, [mload, 64 <c>]], 5 <5>, 1 <msg.value | 2 (msg.value|2)>] ``` ## Impact The wrong value goes wherever the expression is used: storage writes, arithmetic, array indexes, return values and event fields. For example, `self.deposits[msg.sender] = (msg.value | 1) if flag else msg.value` records every deposit made with `flag` set as `1`, so the funds stay in the contract and nobody can withdraw them.

GHSA-cw3h-xwxq-8cx2.title: Ternary expressions misread nested arrays with different inner bounds
GHSA-cw3h-xwxq-8cx2.description: ## Summary When a ternary selects between nested arrays with different inner bounds, selecting the narrower array can corrupt the result. The compiler reads it using the wider array's memory layout without first converting it. Inner arrays after the first are therefore read at the wrong offsets. This can silently produce incorrect values at all optimization levels. The equivalent `if`/`else` assignment gives the correct result. ## Details In Vyper 0.4.3, `parse_IfExp` (`vyper/codegen/expr.py:781-802`) returns a pointer to the selected branch, labelled with the ternary's result type. When both branches are in memory, it leaves their layouts unchanged. In the PoC below, each inner array in `narrow` occupies 96 bytes: a 32-byte length followed by space for two values. The result type reserves 160 bytes per inner array, allowing four values. `_get_element_ptr_array` in `vyper/codegen/core.py` uses that wider spacing, so it reads the second inner array 64 bytes past its actual start. Fixed on `master` by [`1fb7dfe2` (#5236)](https://github.com/vyperlang/vyper/commit/1fb7dfe2). The fix copies branches with incompatible layouts into memory using the result type before returning their pointers. Affected versions: 0.3.8 (which introduced ternaries) through 0.5.0b1. ## PoC ```vyper remaining: public(DynArray[DynArray[uint256, 4], 4]) @external def set(flag: bool, narrow: DynArray[DynArray[uint256, 2], 4], wide: DynArray[DynArray[uint256, 4], 4]): self.remaining = narrow if flag else wide ``` `set(True, [[6, 4], [7, 3]], [])` stores `[[6, 4], [0, 0, 0]]`. The compiler mistakes `narrow[1][1]`, which holds `3`, for the second inner array's length, then reads three zero values from unused memory. An `if`/`else` assignment stores the expected `[[6, 4], [7, 3]]`. Returning `narrow if flag else wide` as the wider type produces the same corrupted result. ## Impact Contracts can silently store or use corrupted values when the misread array lengths remain within bounds, as in this PoC. If a misread length exceeds its bound, the call can revert, depending on how the array is used.

GHSA-fxg7-4wqg-c8gh.title: `create_from_blueprint` offset validation bypass through unsigned wraparound
GHSA-fxg7-4wqg-c8gh.description: ## Summary Vyper's `create_from_blueprint` can deploy a contract with empty runtime bytecode instead of reverting when supplied with an invalid `code_offset`. Contracts that allow attackers to control this parameter are affected. ## Details The builtin computes the remaining blueprint code size using EVM subtraction, then validates the result with a signed comparison: ```python codesize = ['sub', ['extcodesize', target], code_offset] check_codesize = ['assert', ['sgt', codesize, 0]] ``` Because `code_offset` is a `uint256`, subtraction can wrap modulo `2^256` and produce a small positive result that passes the check. For example, given a blueprint with 200 bytes of code: ```text code_offset = 2^256 - 1 codesize = 200 - (2^256 - 1) mod 2^256 = 201 sgt(201, 0) = true ``` `EXTCODECOPY` then reads beyond the blueprint's code and fills the destination with zeros. The resulting initcode begins with `STOP`, so contract creation succeeds and returns an address with no runtime code. The oversized source offset does not itself cause excessive gas consumption. ## Impact An attacker who controls `code_offset` can cause a factory to deploy empty contracts instead of the intended blueprint instances. Depending on the application, this can disrupt initialization, violate assumptions about deployed contracts, or leave ETH and tokens sent to those addresses inaccessible. The common pattern using a fixed, valid offset such as `code_offset=3` is unaffected by this bypass. ## Remediation Validate **`code_offset < extcodesize(target)` using an unsigned comparison before subtraction**. Checking only the wrapped result, even with an unsigned comparison, does not prevent the bypass. As a workaround, use a fixed, valid offset or explicitly enforce this bound before calling `create_from_blueprint`.

GHSA-r3c7-7xwm-6vfw.title: Multi-byte identifier characters can silently change literal values
GHSA-r3c7-7xwm-6vfw.description: ## Summary A multi-byte character, such as a non-ASCII identifier or a byte-order mark, shifts Vyper's source lookup for later literals on the same line. Crafted source can make numeric literals compile with values or types that are not the ones written, without a compiler warning. ## Details In `vyper/ast/parse.py`, `line_index` counts characters, but Python's `col_offset` counts UTF-8 bytes within the line. Each multi-byte character shifts later source slices on that line right by its extra bytes. `visit_Num` classifies literals and reconstructs hexadecimal, binary and decimal values from these slices. A replacement placed where the slice lands therefore becomes the compiled value, and a plain integer can become a hex literal. Two triggers are reachable: - Non-ASCII identifiers that NFKC-normalize to ASCII, such as `ﬁ`, `ｆｏｏ` or `𝚏𝚘𝚘`. - A byte-order mark at the start of the file, which shifts literals on line 1. It is invisible. This shares its root cause with [GHSA-wvx7-39qj-2g9v](https://github.com/vyperlang/vyper/security/advisories/GHSA-wvx7-39qj-2g9v): the line table introduced in 0.4.1. ## Proof of concept The identifier uses mathematical monospace letters (4 bytes, 1 character each). They shift the lookup onto the address in the trailing comment: ```python import vyper # The identifier uses MATHEMATICAL MONOSPACE letters (4 UTF-8 bytes each), # which Python normalizes to the ASCII name TREASURY_ADDRESS_FOR_FEES. source = '''𝚃𝚁𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝚈_𝙰𝙳𝙳𝚁𝙴𝚂𝚂_𝙵𝙾𝚁_𝙵𝙴𝙴𝚂: constant(address) = 0x000000000000000000000000000000000000dEaD # 0x00000000000000000000000000000000c0Ffee11 @external @view def treasury() -> address: return TREASURY_ADDRESS_FOR_FEES ''' # Same contract with an ASCII identifier clean = source.replace(source.split(':')[0], 'TREASURY_ADDRESS_FOR_FEES', 1) # The getter's runtime bytecode matches an explicitly substituted contract. substituted = clean.replace( '0x000000000000000000000000000000000000dEaD', '0x00000000000000000000000000000000c0Ffee11', 1, ) def runtime(code): return vyper.compile_code(code, output_formats=['bytecode_runtime'])['bytecode_runtime'] assert runtime(source) == runtime(substituted) assert runtime(source) != runtime(clean) ``` Both assertions pass. ## Impact An attacker able to contribute source code can change an address, selector, byte sequence, integer or decimal constant. Identifier triggers can pass as ordinary letters in review; a byte-order mark is invisible. ## Affected versions | pip range | Notes | | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `>= 0.1.0b1, < 0.1.0b12` | Literals are read using Python's byte offsets. | | `= 0.1.0b14` | A parser refactor overwrites the `asttokens` character offsets with Python's byte offsets. | | `>= 0.4.1` | Affected through 0.5.0b1; also unpatched on the inspected `master` checkout (`17e925db`). | 0.1.0b12, 0.1.0b13 and 0.1.0b15 through 0.4.0 use character offsets from `asttokens` and are unaffected. ## Remediation Convert byte offsets to character offsets using each line's own text before slicing, and take literal values from the parser instead of source text. Until fixed, reject non-ASCII characters outside comments and docstrings, including a byte-order mark.
